Nangra assamensis Sen & Biswas, 1994. Family Sisoridae. Maximum size 92 mm SL. IUCN status: Least Concern (last assessed 2009).

Type locality: Brahmaputra River at Neematighat, 14 kilometres from Jorhat, Assam, India.
Asia: India. Found in North Eastern India waters (Padma, Jamuna, Brahmaputra), the Ganges and Bengal waters including West Bengal.
Asia: Ganges and Brahmaputra Rivers in India. Type locality: Brahmaputra R. at Neematighat, 14 km from Jorhat, Assam, India. Also occurs in Nepal.

An aquarium having a tight fitting cover glass is best, as they do have a tendency to regularly swim vigorously from the substrate to the surface of the water.

It is essential that good filtration is provided; an internal power filter with quite a good flow of water, and an air diffuser fitted, is recommended in order to provide turbulent and well oxygenated water, which is a must if one wants to keep Nangra assamensis alive and healthy for any length of time.

A substrate of fine rounded gravel interspersed with stones and rocks and a few clumps of short hard-leafed plants would go some way in making this small sisorid feel secure.
Feeding is not too problematic, as it takes well to the usual frozen foods such as daphnia and bloodworms.

Description: Dorsal spines (total): 1; dorsal soft rays (total): 6; vertebrae: 35–37. Dorsal fin with 6 branched rays; dorsal and pectoral-fin spines with filamentous extensions. Anal fin with 4–5 simple rays, 7–9 branched rays. Snout strongly projecting. Head, body and caudal peduncle slightly more elongate than other congeners.

Etymology: The genus name Nangra is tautonymous with Pimelodus nangra, presumably a local Bengali name for this fish along the Kosi River in India. The specific name assamensis: -ensis, suffix denoting place: Assam, India, type locality.

Like other members of the Sisorid family, Nangra possess an adhesive apparatus in the form of visible pleats of skin on their ventral surfaces.

IUCN Red List: assessed as Least Concern (IUCN 2010), but needs updating. It is known from larger rivers in the Ganges and Brahmaputra drainages and has no significant known threats.
Records of the Zoological Survey of India v. 94 (nos 2-4), pp 441, Fig 1; Pl. 1.
